chunks.text: Can you read this?
Did you understand it right away?
If you hesitated, you are not alone.
844,000 adults in Switzerland struggle with reading.
Letters like these decide their money, their deadlines, their rights.
For them, there is easy language.
But easy-language versions are slow expert work.
Leicht·Facile drafts them with Apertus, the Swiss open model,
and gives the writers a checked first draft.
Here is how, on one sentence from a real letter.
Sixteen words. Nobody acts. The verb comes last.
Apertus first takes out what must survive: the deadline, and what you must do.
Then it writes short sentences. Who does what. One thing each.
A middle dot splits long words into easier parts.
Code checks that the date is still there, exactly.
The same for the whole letter.
A larger Apertus model judges the meaning; only flagged sentences are repaired.
Every sentence links to its source, and the writer approves each one.
A strong single prompt, in its default mode, lost almost a quarter of the hard facts, without a word.
Leicht·Facile lists every missing fact.
Easy language matters most in the most personal letters.
A child protection decision for a person with a learning disability. A letter from the hospital. A tax assessment.
Under secrecy, they may not go to a foreign cloud.
Closed models stay with their makers.
Most open models keep their training data closed.
Most fully open ones are built abroad.
Apertus is open down to its data, built and trained in Switzerland, and runs in-house.
For these letters, it is the only option.
Can you read it now?
Now you can.
